lead: This unit turns AC into DC with diodes and thyristors and then judges how good that DC is. By the end you can find the average and RMS output of single-phase and three-phase rectifiers with R, RL and RLE loads, size a filter or a voltage doubler, work out displacement factor, ripple and harmonic factor, allow for source inductance, fix the inverter angle limit, and explain dual converters and PFC front ends.
about: The unit follows the AC-to-DC converter from a plain diode bridge to a grid-friendly rectifier. It starts with the uncontrolled circuits: half-wave, centre-tap and bridge rectifiers, the capacitor and LC filters that smooth them, the voltage doubler and the three-phase diode bridge. Thyristors then bring phase control, first in single-phase circuits (one and two pulses) and then in the three-pulse and six-pulse three-phase converters. The performance chapter gives the language for judging all of them: form and ripple factor, displacement, distortion and harmonic factor, power factor and how to improve it. Source inductance and overlap come next, then inversion and the limit on the firing angle that overlap and turn-off time impose. Two bridges back to back make a dual converter, and the unit ends with the PFC rectifier that makes the input current a sine.

chapters.idea: A diode rectifier gives a fixed average DC voltage decided only by the supply peak and the circuit shape, not by any control.
chapters.depth: Half-wave with R and RL load: waveforms, Vdc = Vm/π, ripple factor 1.21, PIV = Vm, output ripple at f. Centre-tap full-wave: two diodes, Vdc = 2Vm/π, PIV = 2Vm. Bridge: four diodes, same Vdc as centre-tap, PIV = Vm, no centre tap needed. Derive average and RMS output for each, form factor 1.11 for full-wave, ripple factor 0.482, output ripple at 2f. Compare transformer utilisation factor and diode count. Some syllabi call the centre-tap circuit a two-pulse rectifier and write p = 2; a few call the bridge a full-wave bridge to separate it from the centre-tap type. Show the RL case: current stays positive, output voltage clips at zero.

figure.title: Three diode rectifiers
figure.aria: One AC supply feeding three rectifier options, with diode count and peak inverse voltage written under each.
figure.caption: All three give the same average output for a given peak, but the centre-tap circuit needs a transformer with twice the peak inverse voltage per diode.

chapters.example: A single-phase bridge rectifier feeds R = 100 Ω from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. Find Vm, Vdc, Idc, Vrms, Irms, the ripple factor, the PIV of each diode and the output ripple frequency. Answers: Vm = 230√2 = 325.3 V; Vdc = 2Vm/π = 207.1 V; Idc = 2.07 A; Vrms = Vm/√2 = 230 V; Irms = 2.30 A; ripple factor = 0.482; PIV = 325.3 V; ripple at 100 Hz.
chapters.trap: Quoting the full-wave ripple factor 0.482 for a half-wave circuit, whose ripple factor is 1.21, and giving the centre-tap PIV as Vm instead of 2Vm.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: diode V-I characteristic and static resistance.
chapters.leave: Filter design goes to 2.2; firing-angle control to 2.3; three-phase versions to 2.4.

chapters.idea: A capacitor stores charge near the supply peak and a series inductor blocks the ripple, so both turn a pulsating DC into a steadier one at the cost of narrow, tall diode current pulses.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter; keep it short. Shunt capacitor filter across the load: charging near the peak, discharge through R, the approximate ripple Vr = Idc/(2fC) for full-wave and Idc/(fC) for half-wave, and why the capacitor filter suits light loads. Rise in Vdc towards Vm, narrowing of the conduction angle, and the resulting high peak repetitive diode current and unchanged PIV. Series L filter and the L-C filter, bleeder resistor, and the two-stage view of ripple reduction. State the assumptions of each approximate formula instead of deriving them fully.

figure.aria: A curve falling steeply and then flattening, showing ripple voltage against filter capacitance for a 2 A load at 50 Hz.
figure.caption: Ripple falls as 1/C: doubling the capacitor halves the ripple, so large capacitors buy little after a point.

chapters.example: A bridge rectifier on 230 V, 50 Hz feeds a load drawing Idc = 2 A through a 1000 µF capacitor. Estimate the ripple and the DC output. Vr = Idc/(2fC) = 2/(2 × 50 × 1000 × 10⁻⁶) = 20 V. Vdc ≈ Vm − Vr/2 = 325.3 − 10 = 315.3 V.
chapters.trap: Using 2f in the ripple formula for a half-wave rectifier, and forgetting that the capacitor raises Vdc but also raises the diode peak current.
chapters.leave: Regulated supplies and switched-mode converters to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A voltage doubler gives about 2Vm from two diodes and two capacitors; a three-phase diode bridge gives 1.35 VL with 4 % ripple.
Replacing diodes with thyristors and delaying the firing by angle α lets you set the average output voltage continuously, from full positive down through zero to negative.
chapters.depth: Half-controlled (semi) bridge with two SCRs and two diodes, fully controlled bridge with four SCRs, single-phase half-wave controlled circuit. Loads: pure R, RL, and RLE with a back EMF. Continuous against discontinuous conduction, extinction angle β, and boundary between the two. Key results for continuous current: Vdc = (2Vm/π)cos α for the fully controlled bridge; for discontinuous R load Vdc = (Vm/π)(1 + cos α); half-controlled bridge with R load gives (Vm/π)(1 + cos α) and never a negative output. Effect of a freewheeling diode on the RL load. α measured from the natural commutation point, two-pulse operation, and the first mention of inverter mode when α > 90° with a current path. Some syllabi write full converter and semi converter; a few use the word one-quadrant and two-quadrant for these circuits.

figure.aria: Three cosine-shaped curves of normalised average output against firing angle, the continuous-current curve passing through zero at 90 degrees.
figure.caption: Only the continuous-current curve crosses zero and goes negative; the pure-resistance curve stays positive and reaches zero only at 180 degrees.

chapters.example: A single-phase fully controlled bridge works from 230 V, 50 Hz with R = 10 Ω and α = 60°. With continuous current Vdc = (2Vm/π)cos α = 207.1 × 0.5 = 103.5 V and Idc = 10.35 A. With a pure R load the current is discontinuous and Vdc = (Vm/π)(1 + cos α) = 103.5 × 1.5 = 155.3 V, Idc = 15.53 A.
chapters.trap: Using the continuous-current formula for a pure resistance load, and measuring α from the supply zero crossing instead of from the point where the device would naturally start conducting.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 SCR turning on and commutation; 2.1 for diode behaviour at α = 0.
chapters.leave: Source inductance and overlap to 2.6; dual converters to 2.7.

chapters.idea: A three-phase converter draws smoother current and delivers an output whose ripple is at p times the supply frequency, with p the pulse number.
chapters.depth: Three-pulse (half-wave, M3) and six-pulse (bridge, B6) controlled rectifiers. For continuous current: six-pulse Vdc = (3√3 Vm/π)cos α = 1.35 VL cos α, where Vm is phase peak and VL the line RMS; three-pulse Vdc = 1.17 Vph cos α. R, RL and RLE loads, the 60° conduction of each device in the bridge, and the 120° conduction of each device for the three-pulse circuit. Ripple frequency 6f and 3f, α range 0 to 180° for the bridge in inverter mode. Discontinuous conduction on light R load at large α, described briefly without full derivation. Supply transformer connection and the reason the bridge needs no neutral.

figure.aria: Six horizontal bars offset by 60 degrees, each 120 degrees long, showing when each thyristor of a six-pulse bridge conducts.
figure.caption: Each thyristor conducts for 120 degrees and a new pair takes over every 60 degrees, so the output ripple is six times the supply frequency.

chapters.example: A three-phase fully controlled bridge runs from a 400 V, 50 Hz line with continuous current and α = 30°. Vdc = 1.35 × 400 × cos 30° = 1.35 × 400 × 0.866 = 467.6 V. Ripple frequency = 6 × 50 = 300 Hz. For comparison a three-pulse circuit at the same α gives Vdc = 1.17 × (400/√3) × 0.866 = 234 V.
chapters.trap: Putting the line RMS voltage into the formula that expects phase peak, and forgetting that 1.35 already contains the √3 and the √2.
chapters.prereq: 2.3 for firing-angle control; three-phase supply phasors.
chapters.leave: Harmonic and power factor analysis to 2.5; overlap to 2.6.

chapters.idea: The quality of a rectifier is described by a small set of ratios: how much ripple rides on the average, and how much of the input current is useful fundamental.
chapters.depth: Definitions with formulas and typical values: average and RMS output, ripple factor RF = √((Vrms/Vdc)² − 1), form factor, transformer utilisation factor, crest factor. Input side: displacement factor cos φ1 between the fundamental input current and the voltage, distortion factor = I1/Irms, total harmonic distortion THD = √((1/DF)² − 1), and power factor = (I1/Irms)cos φ1 = DF × displacement factor. Harmonic order: odd only for a symmetric bridge, h = kp ± 1 for a p-pulse converter, amplitude falling as 1/h, ripple frequency p·f. Show PF for a single-phase bridge with a square input current and a fully controlled bridge at finite α. Some syllabi say harmonic factor where others say THD; a few write distortion index.

figure.title: Harmonics of a square input current
figure.aria: A table of harmonic orders one, three, five, seven, nine with amplitudes falling as one over h.
figure.caption: A symmetric square wave contains only odd harmonics, each of amplitude 1/h of the fundamental.

chapters.example: A single-phase bridge draws a square input current of peak 10 A and the displacement angle is zero. Find the fundamental RMS, distortion factor, THD and power factor. Fundamental peak = 4I/π = 12.73 A, fundamental RMS = 9.0 A, total RMS = 10 A. DF = 9.0/10 = 0.90. THD = √(1/0.90² − 1) = 0.484, that is 48.4%. PF = 0.90 × 1 = 0.90.
chapters.trap: Reporting displacement factor as the power factor, and listing even harmonics that a symmetric bridge current does not contain.
chapters.prereq: 2.3 and 2.4 for the waveforms whose numbers are being computed; Fourier series basics.
chapters.leave: Filtering of harmonics to 2.2, mitigation by PFC to 2.8.

chapters.idea: The supply has inductance, so current cannot jump from one thyristor to the next; a short overlap period appears, and the output loses a voltage that grows with load current.
chapters.depth: Commutation inductance Ls, overlap angle µ, and the two-phase short circuit during overlap. Average voltage drop: ΔVd = 2ωLs Idc/π for the single-phase bridge and 3ωLs Idc/π for the three-phase bridge, where ω = 2πf. Reduction of the effective firing range, the flat-topped notches in the supply voltage, and the inverter angle limit: the turn-off must finish before the voltage reverses, so α + µ ≤ 180° − δ, with δ the margin angle fixed by the thyristor turn-off time tq. Qualitative link between µ, Idc, Ls and α. Some syllabi call Ls the commutating reactance and write the drop as a per-unit reactance.

figure.aria: A flat line at 540 V and a falling line that starts at the same point and drops about 0.3 V per ampere.
figure.caption: Source inductance leaves the no-load voltage unchanged but makes the output droop as load current rises.

chapters.example: A three-phase bridge works from a 400 V, 50 Hz line with source inductance 1 mH per phase and Idc = 20 A. ω = 2π × 50 = 314 rad/s, ωLs = 0.314 Ω. ΔVd = 3ωLs Idc/π = 3 × 0.314 × 20/π = 6.0 V. At α = 0 the ideal 540 V becomes 534 V.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that the drop appears even at α = 0 and grows with current, and blaming the load inductance, which smooths current but causes no overlap.
chapters.prereq: 2.3 and 2.4 for firing-angle operation; inductance and inductor voltage v = L di/dt.
chapters.leave: The margin angle and device turn-off time are introduced in Unit 1; inverter circuits in Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Beyond 90° a fully controlled converter inverts; overlap and turn-off time limit the firing angle to 180° − μ − γ0.
Two fully controlled bridges facing each other give current in both directions and voltage of both signs, which is what a reversing DC drive needs.
chapters.depth: Converter P and converter N connected back to back through an intergroup reactor. Setting α2 = 180° − α1 so the two average voltages match. Non-circulating mode, where only one bridge conducts at a time and a dead time is needed at reversal, against circulating-current mode, where both conduct and the reactor limits the circulating current. Four-quadrant operation and the ideal relation V1 = −V2. Briefly state why a real dual converter must block the circulating path or limit it. Applications: reversible rolling-mill and crane drives.

figure.title: Dual converter
figure.aria: Two converters joined at a common load, one controlling forward current and the other reverse current, both fed from the same AC supply.
figure.caption: In non-circulating mode only one converter fires at a time; the other waits with its firing angle held at 180° minus the first.

chapters.example: A dual converter feeds R = 5 Ω from 230 V, 50 Hz with α1 = 30°. Converter P: V1 = (2 × 325.3/π)cos 30° = 207.1 × 0.866 = 179.4 V, so I = 35.9 A. Converter N is set to α2 = 150°: V2 = 207.1 × cos 150° = −179.4 V, matching V1 in magnitude and opposite in sign.
chapters.trap: Setting both firing angles equal, and assuming both bridges conduct together when the mode is non-circulating.
chapters.prereq: 2.3 for the fully controlled bridge; Unit 1 for commutation.
chapters.leave: Motor speed control and four-quadrant drive dynamics belong to a drives course; cyclo and matrix converters to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A diode bridge with a capacitor draws short, peaky current; a PFC stage forces the input current to follow the sine voltage so the rectifier looks like a resistor to the grid.
chapters.depth: Why a capacitor-input rectifier has a poor power factor and high THD even though its displacement factor is near one. Passive PFC: series inductor, its size and its limits. Active boost PFC: diode bridge followed by a boost cell, the inner current loop that makes iin proportional to |vin|, the outer slow voltage loop, and the multiplier that sets the current reference. Continuous and discontinuous conduction modes, the 400 V bus for a 230 V mains, the 100 Hz ripple on the output, PF near 0.99 and THD under 5%. A line on bridgeless and interleaved versions, and on grid harmonic standards.

figure.title: Boost PFC front end
figure.aria: A power path from mains through a bridge and a boost cell to a 400 V bus, with a control loop sensing the bus voltage and firing the switch.
figure.caption: The inner loop makes the current follow the rectified sine; the outer loop only decides how large that sine should be.

chapters.example: A 500 W PFC rectifier runs from 230 V, 50 Hz with power factor 0.99 and a 400 V output bus. Input RMS current = 500/(0.99 × 230) = 2.2 A, peak 3.1 A. At the input peak the boost switch duty is D = 1 − 325.3/400 = 0.19, and it rises towards 1 near the zero crossings of the mains.
chapters.trap: Thinking a capacitor filter improves power factor (it makes it worse), and treating power factor correction as only a displacement-angle problem.
chapters.prereq: 2.5 for displacement factor, distortion factor and THD; Unit 3 for the boost converter.
chapters.leave: Boost converter design and control loops to Unit 3; harmonic standards and compliance testing are outside this unit.
